# Part IV: Reasoning and Test-Time Compute {#part-reasoning .unnumbered}

> "... generating a chain of thought ... significantly improves the ability of large
> language models to perform complex reasoning."
>
> Jason Wei et al., ["Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903)

Reasoning in modern models is easiest to misunderstand when it is treated as a
new organ inside the network. This part takes the more useful view: reasoning is
a way of spending computation before the answer is fixed. Sometimes that spending
happens in the prompt. Sometimes it is organized as search. Sometimes it is
delegated to a program, solver, or proof checker. Sometimes it is trained into
the model. Sometimes it remains at inference, where the system samples, checks,
branches, or routes by difficulty before committing.

@sec-eliciting-reasoning begins with the smallest move, giving the model room to
think and refusing to trust a single sample. @sec-structured-reasoning-search
then makes the control problem explicit: a chain is one path, a tree keeps
alternatives alive, and a graph reuses partial work. @sec-programs-solvers-symbolic
splits reasoning into translation and execution, where the model writes a
program, query, symbolic chain, or proof script and an external runtime computes
or checks it. @sec-verifiers-process-supervision studies the verifier itself,
from unit tests and answer checkers to process reward models and generative
verifiers.

@sec-training-to-reason moves the cost into training, where verifiable rewards,
GRPO/RLOO-style optimization, and reinforcement learning try to make useful
reasoning habitual rather than ad hoc. @sec-reasoning-data-distillation treats
the traces as data: self-generated rationales, rejection sampling, small curated
sets, distillation, and long-to-short transfer. @sec-inference-time-scaling then
treats computation at test time as a budgeted resource: parallel attempts,
sequential refinement, verification, routing by difficulty, and the production
problem of overthinking.

The practical test for any reasoning claim is therefore concrete: where is the
extra work paid for, who checks it, what data records it, and does more
computation improve coverage, selection, or both. Once those questions are
separated, the difference between a prompting method, a reasoning-trained model,
and a test-time scaling system becomes an engineering choice rather than a
mystery.
